title: The Balanced Scorecard
author: Robert S. Kaplan and David P. Norton
theme: Financial results alone cannot steer a modern company; strategy must be translated into a balanced set of linked measures that people can act on.
summary: Robert Kaplan and David Norton start from a problem every manager knows. Traditional accounting reports tell you how the business performed last quarter, but they say little about whether it is building the capabilities that will create value next year. In an economy driven by customers, knowledge and innovation, steering only by financial figures is like driving while looking in the rear-view mirror.

Their answer is the balanced scorecard, a framework that keeps financial measures but adds three other perspectives. The customer perspective asks how the firm creates value for the segments it chooses to serve. The internal business process perspective identifies the few processes the company must excel at to satisfy those customers. The learning and growth perspective covers the people, systems and culture that make improvement possible.

The measures are not a random collection of indicators. Each scorecard should tell the story of a strategy through a chain of cause and effect: better skills improve processes, better processes delight customers, and loyal customers produce financial results. The authors also insist on a mix of outcome measures, which show what happened, and performance drivers, which signal what is likely to happen.

The book then moves beyond measurement to management. The scorecard becomes the backbone of four processes: clarifying and translating the vision into concrete objectives, communicating strategy and linking it to team and personal goals, aligning budgets and targets with strategic initiatives, and creating feedback so leaders can test and adjust the strategy itself rather than only checking whether plans were followed.

The lasting lesson is that what gets measured shapes what people pay attention to. A short, well-chosen set of balanced measures turns an abstract strategy into everyday work, and gives the whole organisation a shared language for discussing where it is going and how it will get there.
takeaway: Translate strategy into a few linked measures across finance, customers, processes and learning, then use them to manage, not just to report.

questions.q: What core weakness of traditional performance measurement do Kaplan and Norton highlight?
options: It measures too many non-financial factors
It relies on backward-looking financial figures that ignore future value creation
It is too expensive to collect
It ignores shareholder returns
questions.why: Financial reports describe past results but reveal little about the capabilities that drive future performance.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four perspectives of the balanced scorecard?
options: Financial
Customer
Learning and growth
Competitor
questions.why: The four perspectives are financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth.

questions.q: What does the internal business process perspective focus on?
options: The critical processes the firm must excel at to deliver value to customers
Employee satisfaction surveys only
Quarterly earnings forecasts
Regulatory compliance reports
questions.why: It identifies the few processes that matter most for meeting customer and financial objectives.

questions.q: How should the measures on a scorecard relate to one another?
options: They should be independent so each can be judged alone
They should all be financial ratios
They should be linked in cause-and-effect chains that tell the story of the strategy
They should change every month
questions.why: The authors want measures connected so that improvements in drivers flow through to customer and financial outcomes.

questions.q: The learning and growth perspective is mainly concerned with:
options: Market share growth
Revenue per product line
People, information systems and organisational culture
Mergers and acquisitions
questions.why: It covers the intangible foundations that enable process improvement and innovation.

questions.q: Why do the authors combine outcome measures with performance drivers?
options: Outcomes show results achieved, while drivers signal what is likely to happen
Drivers are easier to audit than outcomes
Outcomes are only for investors
Regulators require both types
questions.why: Lagging outcome measures confirm results; leading driver measures give early warning and direction.

questions.q: Beyond measurement, how do Kaplan and Norton see the scorecard being used?
options: As a replacement for the annual report
As a tool to set executive salaries only
As a marketing document for customers
As a strategic management system that guides communication, planning and learning
questions.why: The book argues the scorecard should anchor key management processes, not just report numbers.

questions.q: Linking the scorecard to team and individual goals mainly helps to:
options: Reduce headcount
Align everyday work with the organisation's strategy
Eliminate the need for budgets
Replace performance reviews
questions.why: Cascading objectives lets employees see how their work contributes to strategic aims.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the feedback and learning process in the scorecard approach?
options: To test and adjust the strategy itself, not only check whether plans were met
To punish managers who miss targets
To collect customer complaints
To audit financial statements
questions.why: Strategic feedback lets leaders question whether their assumptions about cause and effect still hold.

questions.q: Which idea best captures the book's overall message?
options: Profit is the only measure that matters
Measurement is a job for accountants alone
A balanced, linked set of measures turns strategy into action
Strategy should be kept confidential within the board
questions.why: The scorecard translates abstract strategy into measurable objectives that everyone can act on.
